title: OpenAI employee takes down ChatGPT-coded RuneScape clone following Jagex cease-and-desist
author: Ted Litchfield
text:
OpenAI employee Rohan Varma has taken down the browser-based, AI-coded RuneScape clone called Elderwood following negative attention from the RuneScape community and a cease-and-desist request from developer Jagex.
Varma did not post video footage of Elderwood in action, but screenshots on his X profile (via Eurogamer ) show a game with extremely similar graphics and UI to Old School RuneScape. Elderwood further had identical place names to OSRS, including the celebrated Lumbridge, and Varma explicitly described it as an OSRS clone in some of his posts. Varma is a developer on OpenAI's Codex project, a coding-focused AI tool he used to build Elderwood.
Varma uploaded his first X post about Elderwood on September 6. On September 7, user Nutty103X shared a post to the OSRS subreddit calling attention to Elderwood. Nutty103X called for Jagex to C&D the clone game, and most commenters expressed similar sentiments or criticism of Elderwood's quality and originality. On the same day, Varma shared a post noting "a spike in users earlier today because we accidentally went viral on the OSRS subreddit."
According to Eurogamer, Elderwood was taken down at some point on September 9, with the browser-based game replaced with a farewell message from Varma . "We received a notice from Jagex asking us to take down the website," the message reads. "Following that notice, we are discontinuing Elderwood’s operation, and the game is no longer available.
"Elderwood began as a browser-based multiplayer adventure inspired by RuneScape. In a few short days, it grew into a shared world of exploration, skilling, quests, trading and duels—shaped along the way by the people who showed up to play and share ideas."
Some interesting stats about the RuneScape clone I launched yesterday (https://t.co/UbLIpSmgQo):- 3,000 people created accounts- At our peak, we had 55 concurrent users player and we're averaging about 35 online players per hour- A collective 1,000+ hours have been spent… pic.twitter.com/dOVTR6s39c September 7, 2026
Varma further thanked players, and said that the site would remain up with a leaderboard of Elderwood's high scores.
The message strikes me as a bit much for a vibe-coded, inferior clone of a game that already exists. Elderwood's launch-to-takedown speedrun reminds me of the fate of so many Nintendo fan games, with the crucial caveat that those are typically noncommercial creative projects, as opposed to a blatantly copyright-infringing advertisement for OpenAI. For another example, id Software making a Mario 3 port on spec to prove they'd mastered fast-scrolling 2D graphics on DOS? That's cool copyright infringement.
I'm awestruck at the truly ham-fisted "move fast, break things" of this particular exercise: OpenAI is a company already under scrutiny for its impact—generally negative—on creativity, creative ownership, and people being able to make a living from making art. Whatever Varma's intentions with this project, he is a representative of OpenAI, and was using Elderwood to demonstrate the company's projects.

html:
OpenAI employee Rohan Varma has taken down the browser-based, AI-coded RuneScape clone called Elderwood following negative attention from the RuneScape community and a cease-and-desist request from developer Jagex.

Varma did not post video footage of Elderwood in action, but screenshots on his X profile (via Eurogamer) show a game with extremely similar graphics and UI to Old School RuneScape. Elderwood further had identical place names to OSRS, including the celebrated Lumbridge, and Varma explicitly described it as an OSRS clone in some of his posts. Varma is a developer on OpenAI's Codex project, a coding-focused AI tool he used to build Elderwood.

Varma uploaded his first X post about Elderwood on September 6. On September 7, user Nutty103X shared a post to the OSRS subreddit calling attention to Elderwood. Nutty103X called for Jagex to C&D the clone game, and most commenters expressed similar sentiments or criticism of Elderwood's quality and originality. On the same day, Varma shared a post noting "a spike in users earlier today because we accidentally went viral on the OSRS subreddit."

According to Eurogamer, Elderwood was taken down at some point on September 9, with the browser-based game replaced with a farewell message from Varma. "We received a notice from Jagex asking us to take down the website," the message reads. "Following that notice, we are discontinuing Elderwood’s operation, and the game is no longer available.

"Elderwood began as a browser-based multiplayer adventure inspired by RuneScape. In a few short days, it grew into a shared world of exploration, skilling, quests, trading and duels—shaped along the way by the people who showed up to play and share ideas."

Varma further thanked players, and said that the site would remain up with a leaderboard of Elderwood's high scores.

The message strikes me as a bit much for a vibe-coded, inferior clone of a game that already exists. Elderwood's launch-to-takedown speedrun reminds me of the fate of so many Nintendo fan games, with the crucial caveat that those are typically noncommercial creative projects, as opposed to a blatantly copyright-infringing advertisement for OpenAI. For another example, id Software making a Mario 3 port on spec to prove they'd mastered fast-scrolling 2D graphics on DOS? That's cool copyright infringement.

I'm awestruck at the truly ham-fisted "move fast, break things" of this particular exercise: OpenAI is a company already under scrutiny for its impact—generally negative—on creativity, creative ownership, and people being able to make a living from making art. Whatever Varma's intentions with this project, he is a representative of OpenAI, and was using Elderwood to demonstrate the company's projects.

Elderwood was an irresponsible exercise in copyright infringement-as-advertising reminiscent of the nonsense coming out of the US White House's social media account, leaving Varma's somber eulogy all the more galling.

title: Wolverine review roundup: Frankly, we're starting to feel a little better about the whole 'PlayStation 5 exclusive' thing
author: Andy Chalk
text:
Reviews for Insomniac's long-awaited Wolverine are out, and, well, it's not great. I mean that in the very literal sense: It's fine—good, even, at least in some ways—but it's not great , and that's a problem for a game that was positioned as one of Sony's biggest PlayStation 5 exclusives of the past few years. The bar was high, and the ol' Canucklehead didn't quite clear it.
This is especially unwelcome news for PlayStation right now, given that its plate is already pretty full with other bad news. The platform's live service travails have gotten so far out of hand that it's managed to kill Destiny 2 , and there's a reasonable expectation that Bungie itself might not be too far behind.
More recently, it pulled a massive botch with Hideo Kojima's Physint that led to the auteur partnering with Xbox on the project instead. Sony may have had its reasons for pulling the plug , but strictly from a PR perspective, that's the kind of self-own that leaves a deep scar. Similarly, the company is taking heat for its decision to end physical disc production in 2028, a move that may be rationally defensible but is nonetheless really pissing a lot of people off .
And now, this: A major PS5 exclusive that's landed with all the grace of an egg chucked at a school bus. Because of its platform exclusivity, we can't tell you what we think of the game, except that we're feeling a little better about not getting it. We can, however, tell you what other sites think of it, so let's do that.
"Missing that crucial X-factor"
GamesRadar : 3/5
GR's Leon Hurley says Wolverine's mid-game feels like the game Insomniac wanted to make: "It's lively, layered, and just a fun place to be." Alas, "the rest of the game feels thin, and largely consists of boxy corridors that top and tail Tokyo with shallow combat luges broken up by cutscene checkpoints and little else."
"Good character work props up flashy combat that wears thin over time"
IGN : 6/10
IGN reviewer Simon Cardy found much to like in Logan's character: "Liam McIntyre’s performance grants Logan a personality to match his trademark blades – a sharp, surprising hidden depth, housed in a bulky, blunt instrument of a body. He delicately balances the shadows of his past with the future of mutantkind, all while managing his Jekyll and Hyde nature, as animal instincts sometimes break through the compassion he strives to show." Actual gameplay, though, "wears thin well before the conclusion."
"Insomniac’s most violent game yet is a globe-trotting Wolverine adventure"
Shacknews : 8/10
Donovan Erskine at Shacknews said Wolverine "does an excellent job adapting the iconic mutant," with "some excellent character moments in what is otherwise a fairly standard comic book story." As others noted, he said combat became "repetitive" as the game progressed, but found it "deeply satisfying" despite that.
(Image credit: Insomniac Games) "A gripping, emotional bloodbath"
DualShockers : 8.5/10
Christian Bognar provided one of the more upbeat takes on Wolverine for DualShockers, writing that Insomniac's portrayal of the character is "a success," thanks to its "deeply personal story that explores what it means to live with trauma, loss, and regret." Christian also felt the combat in Wolverine was a step up from that of Insomniac's previous Spider-Man game, despite lacking Spidey's "freedom and versatility."
"Relentless momentum"
GameInformer : 8.5/10
GI's Matt Miller is clearly a fan, writing that "the high speed, brutal slashing, and unstoppable force of Wolverine are captured better than any film or game to come before." And where many other reviews found the game wore thin before its conclusion, calling it "an intense and unrelenting ride" that "doesn't wear out its welcome."
"Marvel's Wolverine's claw-fueled combat doesn't feel as deep as its systems suggest, but that didn't stop me from grinning ear to ear carving through its lengthy campaign"
TechRadar : 4/5
Writing for TechRadar, review Matt Cabral said Wolverine's fighting mechanics "suffer from a lack of meaningful depth," but praised the game's production values: "Supported by visceral, varied, and extremely violent melee combat, this set-piece-packed, cinema-rivaling spectacle puts you behind the claws – and mutton chops – of the fan-favorite superhero like never before."
"Only aims as high as its stout hero"
GameSpot : 6/10
Tamoor Hussain declared in his take for GameSpot that Wolverine is "a fun but forgettable experience that’ll entertain you for a few hours." But it also demonstrates the limitations of the character himself, especially when compared to the open world and energetic dynamism of the studio's previous Spider-Man games: "Wolverine might be the best at what he does, but what he does hasn’t let Insomniac’s developers be the best at what they do."
"Uninspired gameplay leaves Logan feeling declawed despite a strong narrative:
VGC : 3/5
Like many other reviewers, VGC's Jordan Middler enjoyed Wolverine's characters and story, but found everything the game's "tightly crafted and emotive story moments" to be lacking. "The third-person hacking and slashing is fine, but it barely evolves from hour one until hour twelve," Jordan wrote. And while Wolverine has a handful of other abilities at his disposal, they didn't really add much to the power fantasy and felt "ineffective" compared to Logan's standard moveset.
(Image credit: Insomniac Games) "Uninspired action carried by Logan's puppy-dog charm"
Eurogamer : 3/5
In yet another review that praises the characters and narrative of Wolverine while being cooler on the gameplay, Chris Tapsell wrote that the combat isn't bad, it's just overly repetitive. "After the fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh wave of jump-and-parryable-attack guys comes at you with the exact same cadence of parry timing and bullet-dodging you just start to glaze over a little ... When you're putting your fist through someone's eyes, face, heart and feeling absolutely nothing, it's a sign something's a little off. In the blandest terms: too many of the same enemies, dealt with in the same way, for too long."
"A gloriously conflicted lead is let down by crude, boring battling"
The Guardian : 3/5
Keith Stuart at The Guardian is yet another reviewer who enjoyed Wolverine the character more than Wolverine the game. "Despite the full-bloodied use of Wolverine’s claws and a generous array of moves and combos, combat lacks both the bone-crunching impact of the Batman Arkham games and the balletic joy of Spider-Man. As the game goes on and the enemies line up, it feels increasingly like a chore. Logan becomes what he always dreaded: hired muscle."
(Image credit: Insomniac Games) "A patchwork quilt of ideas from other PlayStation games that frequently bump against each other"
Giant Bomb : 2.5/5
Giant Bomb's Shawn McDowell came in on the lower end of the Wolverine review spectrum—he liked the voice acting and "mostly-good combat," but not much else. "[Spider-man] is all about exploring every nook and cranny of New York through fast, fun web swinging, quietly taking out baddies from the shadows, and frequently getting into street brawls with thugs. If they were going to use that as a template for Wolverine, a character with far fewer tools who isn’t associated with the big city, how would that make sense? Turns out, it often doesn’t."
And a few unscored reviews, just for fun: The Verge says "Wolverine’s bloodthirsty focus on action is something that makes it stand out," Kotaku called it "refreshing in its straightforward focus" but also "stagnant," and Polygon pulled no punches, calling Wolverine "the biggest disappointment of the PS5 era."
Marvel's Wolverine comes out on September 15, and—as we've covered pretty well already—is available exclusively on the PlayStation 5.

title: Modder adds 235 destructible Flock cameras to GTA 5 so you can 'do whatever the flock you want' to them
author: Christopher Livingston
text:
You've no doubt spent dozens of hours in GTA 5 doing millions of dollars of property damage with your fleet of speeding vehicles and arsenal of deadly weapons.
But what if you could do something good for the city of Los Santos while still satisfying your insatiable bloodlust and appetite for destruction? For example, blowing up and running down a couple hundred Flock cameras.
Thanks to the GTALPR mod (which stands for Grand Theft Automated License Plate Reader), you can! The mod adds 235 Flock cameras to GTA 5, and in the modder's words, you can "do whatever the flock you want" to 'em. Shoot 'em. Smash 'em. Take 'em out with cars and tanks and shotguns. And you can even make a tidy profit while fighting back against the surveillance state.
What's especially cool about GTALPR, created by modder Morry, is that these cameras aren't just static props, they actually work. They'll photograph you as you drive past them, and you can save and format these photos for social media or your own scrapbook. The cameras will also alert the cops to your location, sometimes even if you're not breaking any laws—just like real Flock cameras are prone to do, because they suck.
Destroying the Flock cameras drops a bundle of components you can sell for extra cash, a nice bonus at $600 a pop. And if you want to go on a rampage, "there is built-in speedrun functionality, with a stats screen tracking number of cameras destroyed, and fastest time to destroy 10, 50, or all cameras," Morry says. That's rad. The mod also lets you place your own in-game cameras to save snapshots of your exploits around the city.
"Anyway, Flock is a scourge on America," the modder states bluntly on TikTok . "It's a private eight billion dollar surveillance company that operates over 100,000 cameras across the country. If you think the 235 in this mod are bad, just understand that that is literally one tenth of the cameras currently installed in LA County, which Los Santos is based on."
The modder, however, warns at the end of the video that "destroying Flock cameras in real life is illegal and will not, as far as we know, give you a loot box with $600."
Works for me. Learn more about the mod here , and grab it for yourself on Github . And thanks to FRVR for spotting the mod.

title: While still headquartered in the US, Saber exec Tim Willits says it has 'no real development in North America anymore'
author: Ted Litchfield
text:
In a Gamescom interview with GamesIndustry.biz , Saber Interactive CCO Tim Willits revealed that the company has "no real development in North America anymore," with only publishing operations continuing in the region, while game development occurs at a host of global subsidiaries.
"We are not afraid of any territories," Willits said. "Some publishers are afraid to work in territories they don't understand, but we're like, let's go, let's find some people that are talented, let's give them what they need, and let's make awesomeness. You don't need to be in California to be a brilliant programmer or artist or animator."
Willits expressed his disapproval of the "wasted money" he sees in many triple-A games, contrasting an unspecified recent release with Saber's own Space Marine 2. "It was a third [of the cost], and it sold 11 million more copies," Willits boasted.
Baseless speculation lightning round
What game do you think Willits was alluding to? Sound off in the comments. My best guesses are Halo: Campaign Evolved or Marathon, two North American triple-As with sales publicly reported at one million units at last call (to Space Marine's 12 at last check), and budgets well in excess of the 40K shooter's⁠—though difficult to pin down exactly.
"The problem is stuff like this: big North American development studios, they run about $2 million+ in burn rate a month. A month ," said Willits. "SnowRunner, which has made hundreds of millions of dollars, costs us $6 million to make. That's literally three months of development time in California. So just run the math on that. If it takes [a big studio] five years to make a game, that's 60 months, that's $120 million just in salaries."
A large part of what Willits is describing is offshoring jobs to lower-wage markets. GI.biz describes Saber as having development offices in Serbia, Armenia, Georgia, Spain, Portugal, Sweden, Argentina, and Australia.
But he undeniably has a point: Triple-A game development in the United States is clearly unsustainable as currently organized. Speaking with us at Gamescom, Willits diagnosed "overspecialization" among developers as another contributor to the ongoing crisis in the industry, though he also argued the crisis is not quite so bad as it's being reported.

title: Polyarc, developer of the excellent VR platforming series Moss, is shutting down after 12 years: 'We are saying our farewells to each other'
author: Rick Lane
text:
Polyarc, the studio behind the Moss series of VR platformers, has announced it is shutting down, three months on from releasing its latest game on Steam.
"After nearly 12 years riding the joyous rollercoaster of emotions that is making video games, our time together has come to an end," the studio posted on LinkedIn (via IGN ). "As we wind down active development, we are saying our farewells to each other."
Founded in 2015, Polyarc made its video game debut three years later with Moss (now known as Moss: VR). Initially released as a PSVR exclusive, Moss launched onto Steam in June 2018, quickly establishing itself as one of VR's best games.
Unlike most VR games, which naturally focus on first person experiences. Moss took classic third-person platforming and infused it with the unique perspective of VR. Players simultaneously controlled Quill—the game's heroic mouse protagonist—using conventional action/adventure controls, while also overseeing the game's storybook 3D as the reader, VR touch controls to manipulate objects and assist Quill in solving puzzles.
The result was an experience not quite like anything else—at least until the similarly excellent sequel arrived in 2022. Together, both games earned Polyarc over 160 awards and nominations, and were relatively commercially successful, especially on Meta platforms.
In 2025, Polyarc released Glassbreakers: Champions of Moss , a PvP strategy spinoff set in the same universe. However, Glassbreakers seems to have failed to attract much of an audience. Polyarc encountered further struggles later in 2025, losing funding for one mid-development project and failing to secure an alternative 'hail mary' funding deal with a third-party publisher. This culminated in the Polyarc laying off two-thirds of its staff earlier this year.
Polyarc's final release— Moss: The Forgotten Relic —arrived in July. Codeveloped by Blackbird Interactive, The Forgotten Relic is a compilation of the first two Moss games plus the original game's expansion The Twilight Garden, all reworked as a traditional, non-VR experience. Like most of Polyarc's output, the reception to The Forgotten Relic was very positive. However, the game clearly didn't sell well enough to preserve what remained of the studio.
As part of its statement, Polyarc posted a link to a Google spreadsheet listing the 30 developers affected by Polyarc's closure and their contacts, to help with future recruitment: "Working together over all of these years has been an honor. Bringing surprise and delight to those who played our games has been a privilege. Thank you to everyone at Polyarc, our work is now finished."
As Polyarc winds down, all the Moss games (except Glassbreakers) are currently on sale, with The Forgotten Relic at 20% off, and the VR versions of Moss and Moss 2 at half-price. Polyarc, the studio behind the Moss series of VR platformers, has announced it is shutting down, three months on from releasing its latest game on Steam.

"After nearly 12 years riding the joyous rollercoaster of emotions that is making video games, our time together has come to an end," the studio posted on LinkedIn (via IGN). "As we wind down active development, we are saying our farewells to each other."

Founded in 2015, Polyarc made its video game debut three years later with Moss (now known as Moss: VR). Initially released as a PSVR exclusive, Moss launched onto Steam in June 2018, quickly establishing itself as one of VR's best games.

Unlike most VR games, which naturally focus on first person experiences. Moss took classic third-person platforming and infused it with the unique perspective of VR. Players simultaneously controlled Quill—the game's heroic mouse protagonist—using conventional action/adventure controls, while also overseeing the game's storybook 3D as the reader, VR touch controls to manipulate objects and assist Quill in solving puzzles.

The result was an experience not quite like anything else—at least until the similarly excellent sequel arrived in 2022. Together, both games earned Polyarc over 160 awards and nominations, and were relatively commercially successful, especially on Meta platforms.

In 2025, Polyarc released Glassbreakers: Champions of Moss, a PvP strategy spinoff set in the same universe. However, Glassbreakers seems to have failed to attract much of an audience. Polyarc encountered further struggles later in 2025, losing funding for one mid-development project and failing to secure an alternative 'hail mary' funding deal with a third-party publisher. This culminated in the Polyarc laying off two-thirds of its staff earlier this year.

Polyarc's final release—Moss: The Forgotten Relic—arrived in July. Codeveloped by Blackbird Interactive, The Forgotten Relic is a compilation of the first two Moss games plus the original game's expansion The Twilight Garden, all reworked as a traditional, non-VR experience. Like most of Polyarc's output, the reception to The Forgotten Relic was very positive. However, the game clearly didn't sell well enough to preserve what remained of the studio.

As part of its statement, Polyarc posted a link to a Google spreadsheet listing the 30 developers affected by Polyarc's closure and their contacts, to help with future recruitment: "Working together over all of these years has been an honor. Bringing surprise and delight to those who played our games has been a privilege. Thank you to everyone at Polyarc, our work is now finished."

As Polyarc winds down, all the Moss games (except Glassbreakers) are currently on sale, with The Forgotten Relic at 20% off, and the VR versions of Moss and Moss 2 at half-price. While The Forgotten Relic has been well received, if you have a VR headset, it's well worth dusting it off to play both Moss games as they were originally designed to be experienced.

title: Wardogs sold over 1 million copies in its first 24 hours, making its launch a bright spot in an otherwise tough year for multiplayer shooters
author: Rick Lane
text:
All signs have pointed to Wardogs being a hit for a while now. Its beta weekend in August was rapturously received, with half a million players lining up to check out its prerelease playtest. When the game launched into early access last week, so many people rushed to get on board that it collapsed the game's servers .
Now, developer Bulkhead has released its initial sales figures for Wardogs, and they are unsurprisingly very strong. The multiplayer FPS sold 1.25 million copies within 24 hours, and that number is likely to be much higher by now.
Bulkhead played it cool while announcing the milestone, simply thanking players and reassuring them that the studio is "watching everything, monitoring servers, and enjoying watching you play". That middle point is likely made in response to the flurry of negative reviews Wardogs received in the wake of its server troubles.
Nonetheless, it's heartening to see an unambiguous hit in the multiplayer FPS sphere after what has been a difficult year for new competitive shooters. 2026 started badly when Highguard ran directly into a brick wall in January, launching to initially high player counts that quickly plummeted to an unsustainable level—resulting in the game shutting down mere weeks later.
In March, Bungie released Marathon , which is one of my favourite games of this year and a real triumph of both art and game design. Yet despite its qualities, it's pretty clear that Marathon has not been the success that either Bungie or Sony hoped. Despite numerous experiments to revive the game's fortunes, its concurrent player numbers are now significantly lower than those of Destiny 2 —which Bungie rather suddenly wrapped development on earlier this year.
Other promising shooters that failed to attract an audience include Last Flag and Empulse . The former was a fun take on Capture the Flag that sadly never really got off the ground, while the latter was the latest in a rather chaotic run of FPS experiments by Splitgate 2 devs 1047 Games—a spiritual successor to Titanfall which, despite some cool ideas, failed to generate sufficient revenue to justify ongoing development.
All of which makes it reassuring to see Wardogs rush out of the gate so strongly. As for the key to its success, I think it lies in the fact that, despite being a blend of ArmA and Battlefield , Wardogs is actually quite laissez-faire in how it lets you play. You're free to approach its massive 100-player battlefields however you like, and instead of forcing teams to work together, it incentivises cooperative play through using cash as a mechanic. You can offer monetary rewards to other players for all manner of different things, ranging from getting a helicopter ride into battle to bribing medics to revive you when downed .
The big question of course, is whether Wardogs can maintain this momentum. There's a lot of big games still to release this year, including Grand Theft Auto 6 , which is likely to suck up attention on all fronts, and Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 , a more direct competitor to Wardogs. Then again, the fact we can say CoD and Wardogs are in competition at all indicates just how well the latter is doing.

title: CD Projekt wanted to put a chain weapon in The Witcher 3 years ago, but it's taken until Songs of the Past because it was 'impossible to do at the time'
author: Rick Lane
text:
The Witcher 3 's recently revealed expansion Songs of the Past will bring more to CD Projekt's acclaimed fantasy adventure than a new region to explore and quests to pursue, it will also introduce a new weapon for Geralt of Rivia to wield—a gnarly silver chain. Well, "new" might not be a wholly appropriate term for it. Geralt's chain weapon—which appears in the novels—was originally seen in the opening cinematic for 2007's The Witcher, making it one of the earliest things players see in the trilogy. But it hasn't appeared as a tool players can use until now.
Apparently though, CD Projekt has previously considered introducing the chain, having discussed it more than a decade ago during The Witcher 3's original development: "We were talking about implementing the chain even during the original Witcher 3." Jakob Rokosz, Songs of the Past's Game Director, told BBC News (via GamesRadar+ ). "But it was impossible to do at the time for various technological reasons and challenges,
Rokosz didn't go into detail about what those challenges were. But reading between the lines, it sounds like they had to do with the chain's animations or physics engine. "A few things had to click together, because we were actually able to address those challenges and issues," Rokosz explained, noting that they did this during the remastering process for The Witcher 3. "Then we were able to implement a weapon that just feels natural and very fluid and basically realises the fantasy you either read in the books or have seen in the trailer."
But the chain isn't appearing solely because CD Projekt can do it. Senior quest designer Despoina Anetaki, who was also being interviewed by the BBC, explained that the weapon "fits with the narrative theming" of Songs of the Past. "It fits with the new enemies that work with the chain," she continued. "We were able to do crowd control with the swarmions that swarm you and you have to keep them away from you."
Swarmions, I should point out, are a somewhat unimaginatively named new enemy-type coming to Songs of the Past. It also sounds like the chain will act as an alternative to (or outright replacement for) the crossbow introduced in The Witcher 3. Anetaki describes it as "a very cool weapon for players who might be sick of the crossbow by now," suggesting it's designed to play a similar role.
If you want to know more about Geralt's silver chain, our own Joshua Wolens saw the weapon in action at Gamescom last month. Like the crossbow, the chain slows down time when you use it and lets you target specific body parts. Joshua had plenty else to say about Songs of the Past too, like how it focuses on Geralt's friendship with Dandelion, and how much livelier its new region feels than those of the base game and its expansions.

title: Starfinder: Afterlight, a CRPG based on one of my favourite systems that pulled in almost $1 million on Kickstarter, is starting to look ship-shape
author: Harvey Randall
text:
I've been keeping a close eye on Starfinder: Afterlight for a few reasons—firstly, I'm a Pathfinder 2e sicko, and Starfinder 2e works on a ton of the same rules. Secondly, because I love a good CRPG, and thirdly, because this game has a surprising amount of financial and voice acting heft behind it.
After getting a surprising €828,164 (around $960,000) funded out of a humble €75,000 ask on Kickstarter , the game managed to snag Red Dead Redemption's Arthur Morgan for its narration . It also just so happens to be getting voice direction from Neil Newbon, who you might know as Astarion from Baldur's Gate 3 —and the man's voicing an interstellar priest bug, which is as charming as it sounds.
Alongside some promising key art, I was curious to see if Epicteller Game's debut game could put another solid CRPG on the market—and after going through the playtest, I was rendered… cautiously optimistic . What I played was very rough around the edges, missing features, customisation, and so on.
I shan't say its official demo, which is now out on Steam , has quelled my apprehension completely. It has, however, left me feeling like Epictellers can pull this thing together with enough polish, given the marked improvement from the playtest I enjoyed in March.
First up, the bad: It still runs terribly, and doesn't have any graphical settings at all yet, animations for combat are a touch clunky, and you can't make a custom character—which is a huge draw of any CRPG, though you can pick from three custom premades.
It's also a fairly linear demo, and while I'd be a fool to expect the breadth of something like Baldur's Gate 3, it'd still be nice to have a little more space to roam, meaningful NPCs to talk to, and a side quest or two. As it stands, the demo's just a series of hallways connected by story, with a few choices to make.
But in comparison to what I played in March? It's clear that the polishing is being done. The demo opens with a gorgeously-animated intro that sets the space-swashbuckling tone well, as your ship is assailed by the dreaded Corpse Fleet. Your captain, Khali, heroically tackles their leader off a ledge and leaves you to defend a set of escape pods carrying your crewmates.
You crash-land on the backwater of Akiton, and mysteriously, five years have passed—not a terrible setup for an RPG by any means, and much improved by the fact you immediately meet Newbon's effusive and peppy bug priest with a baby strapped to his chest. Don't worry, it's traditional for Shirren, the little guy's fine.
Epictellers Entertainment Epictellers Entertainment Epictellers Entertainment Epictellers Entertainment Epictellers Entertainment Epictellers Entertainment Epictellers Entertainment Epictellers Entertainment And while this game chugs, performance issues can be fixed—the more important part is its aesthetic, which is impressive for a studio of this size. Character portraits are lovingly rendered, the comic-book style cutscenes are cute, and Akiton is bright and colourful, plus will look measurably more so when Epictellers figures out how to get it running at a reasonable framerate.
The voice-acting, for a smaller-scale project, is also charming, if a touch inconsistent, but there's a great marriage of voice talent and spectacular character design for your companions, so the focus is in the right place.
The UI is much-improved, carving up character features and abilities into neat little icons, while also tucking plenty of info for min-maxers like me into nested tooltips. And while the combat in the demo is tethered to low-level play, which isn't exciting in any TTRPG system, I can vouch that it will get more interesting as time goes on. As a Pathfinder 2e freak , the three action system has made an evangelist out of me.
It'll need a better tutorial to pull in the layman, mind. I was merrily applying +1 status bonuses and avoiding the dreaded multiple attack penalty because I'm already deeply familiar with the system. As it stands, though, the game awkwardly hucks a bunch of missable tooltips at you in the right corner of the screen. I don't usually advocate for pop-ups, but given how crunchy Starfinder 2e can be, it wouldn't hurt to hold your hand. Or, at the very least, let you know that spamming attacks won't help you.
It's hard to properly tell the trajectory of any given, early project like this—game development is a monstrously complicated business and I'm working with two data points—but I wouldn't bet against Epictellers being able to get this thing ship-shape in time.

title: BlizzCon 2026 Opening Ceremony recap—what's next for Warcraft, Diablo, and StarCraft
author: Tyler Wilde
text:
BlizzCon 2026 kicked off today with the Opening Ceremony at 10:30 am PT , where we got major announcements about what the next several years hold for Blizzard. The festivities can be viewed in the player above, or on YouTube here.
There were rumors that a new StarCraft game would be announced, and yep, it's an open world shooter but it's still years away. There was also lots of chatter about a possible new spin on World of Warcraft: Classic, which was revealed as WoW: Forever.
I'm on scene at the convention in Anaheim, and cataloged the big news from the Opening Ceremony in the live blog below. Look for deeper coverage on the big announcements on PC Gamer throughout the coming week.
September 12, 2026 – 10:36 AM RTS or FPS?
A StarCraft FPS has been rumored for a bit now, but speculation has also gone on regarding the possibility of a new StarCraft RTS. If you can only have one, which are you picking?
September 12, 2026 – 10:46 AM If there were any doubt...
(Image credit: Future) ...That a StarCraft announcement is imminent, its presence on a huge banner among Blizzard's other major series may put that to rest. I was also handed this mini when I checked in:
(Image credit: Blizzard)
September 12, 2026 – 12:31 PM
(Image credit: Future) The livestream has come to life with an hour to go before showtime. I've opted to cover the Opening Ceremony from my hotel room, because when you get a hotel room with decent wi-fi, you don't want to squander that.
That means I don't have any exciting photos from inside the theater to share, but here's a shot of the crowd working its way through security. (I'm going back to my dim, air conditioned room now.)
September 12, 2026 – 1:08 PM It's all about legacy these days
(Image credit: BlizzCon) It's no accident that there's a CRT monitor on set for this pre-show stream. Microsoft has clearly communicated a desire to return to and build on its past glories. Gears of War: E-Day is an Xbox exclusive on console, there are a bunch of Fallout games in the works, and Bethesda's under pressure to hurry up and get The Elder Scrolls 6 out the door.
Meanwhile, some risky original projects have been cancelled in recent years, namely a ZeniMax MMO and a Blizzard survival game, and the big rumors heading into BlizzCon relate to oldies: StarCraft and World of Warcraft: Classic.
Blizzard is certainly playing around with generative AI behind the scenes: The studio's associate director of applied science, Zhen Zhai, spoke at a GDC panel titled " AI Trends of Today and Opportunities for Tomorrow " that I attended earlier this year. But when facing the public, I think we can expect a lot of this nostalgic imagery, not just from Blizzard but the industry at large. The '90s were fun. Remember Bawlz?
I like the live music performance going on here, with the cool Nord keyboard. I've become a keyboard and synthesizer nerd recently, so I can now say judgey stuff like that I prefer the key action on Yamahas (based on mashing the keys of Guitar Center demo units), but those red Nord chassis are so cool.

title: The Blood of Dawnwalker is a good game, but one change would make it a great RPG
author: Fraser Brown
text:
Dungeon Master
(Image credit: Future) Welcome to Dungeon Master , PC Gamer's regular RPG column, where Online Editor Fraser Brown delves into PC gaming's most beloved and enduring genre. Grab a seat in our badly-lit tavern and please ignore the goblin puke.
The Blood of Dawnwalker is good stuff—over the course of a week I drank deeply and had a grand ol' time walking on walls and carving people up with my monstrous claws. But as a choice-laden RPG that promised a lot of agency, it ended up being a bit of a disappointment. There were plenty of choices to be made, but rarely did they leave an impact on either the world or the white bread protagonist, Coen of Laslea.
Rebel Wolves made Coen in the mold of Geralt of Rivia, in that he's a defined character who you can nudge in different directions, but Coen is no Geralt.
(Image credit: Rebel Wolves) By The Witcher 3 , CDPR had the two previous games to lean on, along with a boat-load of books, which helped the studio create a well-defined, consistent character no matter what choices you made. Coen, on the other hand, is just at the start of his journey , and in Dawnwalker, his defining feature is that he loves his family.
Look, I don't mind Coen. Will de Renzy-Martin gave a good performance, but it's hard to do much with a character who's just a nice boy. And while the writers did some interesting stuff in regards to Coen's childhood trauma and his obligation to his family—is it love, or is he trapped in a prison of responsibility?—he's mostly just a pleasant dude.
The choices players face fall into the traditional binary category, which in this case means you can either choose a Coen who is willing to do everything to save his family except become a monster, or a Coen who is willing to do everything to save his family including becoming a monster—but is still mostly a good egg.
(Image credit: Rebel Wolves) Unfortunately, this changes surprisingly little. If you let a vrakhir collaborator go free or murder them, it might change how you feel about the character you're playing, but the world itself couldn't care less. Until the epilogue, most choices you make happen in the background, in a vacuum, and the choices you'd expect to have the greatest impact, like how you choose to defeat Brencis, are largely detached from the kind of Coen you've been playing for 40 hours.
I played Coen as wholesome and naive, but I still found myself able to get every ending. It just came down to which route to Brencis I decided to settle on at the last moment. How I comported myself had no impact. And even though I tried to be consistent when it came to how I roleplayed Coen, the voice direction would often take things in a very different direction, transforming, for instance, what appeared to be a neutral statement into an angry criticism.
This is something that often bugs me in voice-acted RPGs. The acting and direction can dramatically change the tone of a line in a way that feels incongruous to the rest of the conversation, and this happens so much in Dawnwalker. It's something CDPR deftly resolved in The Witcher by making Geralt incredibly stoic. Doug Cockle has plenty of range, but when he's playing Geralt it's extremely subtle, which maintains the consistency of each dialogue sequence.
Final countdown
(Image credit: Rebel Wolves) But Dawnwalker has something most RPGs don't: a ticking clock. And while the most obvious benefit is the sense of urgency it blesses the game with, it also seemed like a promising roleplaying mechanic—helping players to better define their version of Coen by determining what's most important to him.
This is felt most keenly in the prologue, before Coen becomes a dawnwalker. You have one day to do some chores before everyone in the village has to visit the church to get drained by their undead rulers. It's impossible to do everything . Do you focus on helping your fellow villagers? Or do you spend the day hanging out with your family? What's most important to your Coen?
Even during this single day, there's a tangible sense of time moving inexorably forwards. For instance, early in the day you'll meet your siblings, who want to spend time with you and go down to the river. If you decline initially, later you'll find that they've gone to the river by themselves, and you can meet them down there, or just continue to ignore them. There's a schedule.
(Image credit: Rebel Wolves) This promise of time's fickle nature is largely done away with after you complete the prologue. You have 30 days to finish the game—if you want to save your family, anyway—but within those 30 days any time pressure is just an illusion. You'll meet people on the second day who want your help, and they'll still be waiting around for you by the 25th day.
In my entire playthrough, outside of the prologue, I only encountered a single quest where I ran out of time. I could have caught up with an old friend who joined the rebels, but once I'd completed all the quests for the organisation, they mobilised to take on Brencis, at which point I could no longer hang out with my pal. According to our guide lead Sean Martin, who completed every quest Dawnwalker offered, he only found one other example of this happening.
So I never had to make any tough choices. Do I hang out with the mean vampire lady and learn more about the monster I'm becoming? Or do I have a magical adventure with the friendly witch who wants to help me save my family? It doesn't matter because I can always do both.
Evening plans
(Image credit: Rebel Wolves) There's definitely an argument for making Dawnwalker's time limit 20 days instead of 30, but I think that might make the adventure feel too rushed. Instead, sticking with 30 days but putting individual quests on a timer would make a lot more sense. This forces you to make decisions about how Coen should spend his time every day, as well as giving NPCs more agency, while still letting you do a lot.
Being made to choose between staging a jailbreak or assassinating a high-ranking soldier is a much more effective way to establish who Coen is compared to the extremely common choice of: drink a barrel of blood or smash a barrel of blood. It also leaves room for meaningful consequences—like discovering the terrible fate of the prisoners if you opted to do the assassination mission instead, and having other characters actually reference it.
What's frustrating is that you occasionally see glimmers of this, like the time of day you do a quest subtly changing how things play out.
(Image credit: Rebel Wolves) When I tried to meet up with the rebels for the first time, I played through it twice: once during the day, and once at night. At night, I found a rebel being harassed by soldiers, who were immediately hostile to me. After I quickly murdered the soldiers, the rebel took me to meet her friends, but I sensed a trap thanks to my supernatural skills, and avoided getting my leg stuck in a snare.
Attempting this in the afternoon, I was actually able to talk to the soldiers instead of killing them immediately. Rather than fighting, I bribed them to leave the rebel alone. But when I was brought to meet her fellow rebels, I walked right into the snare trap.
This was cool! Though it didn't actually matter at all. In vampire form, even though I avoided the first trap, the rebels ended up jumping me and chaining me to a tree. No matter the time of day, the end result was the same.
(Image credit: Rebel Wolves) I also randomly encountered one of the vamp bosses in a cathedral I'd broken into one evening, at which point I could take her out there and then—dropping from the rafters and plunging my claws into her.
Discovering that some characters had lives outside of the quests attached to them was neat, though taking her out early actually undermined the narrative—it meant I would have missed out on all the context that made her character more than simply a ghoulish monster. So I killed her, felt badass for taking her out early, and then immediately reloaded an old save—letting her live until I'd completed the quests building up to our final confrontation.
But both of these encounters gave me a glimpse of what could have been: a game where time forces your hand, where NPCs have routines and deadlines, where it genuinely matters if you do a quest at noon or in the wee hours of the morning. A glimpse of a better RPG.
Clockwork
(Image credit: Rebel Wolves) Most of the time, however, when you choose to do a quest only really changes the mechanics you can take advantage of. Which also means, given the choice, you should usually try to do things at night, when you're stronger and can teleport. Anything requiring witchcraft, meanwhile, can only be done during the day, so you're not really making a choice there. In this way, time becomes a largely perfunctory feature.
When that illusion is broken, The Blood of Dawnwalker becomes incredibly familiar: a checklist of tasks peppered across a big map, which you can largely do in whatever order you fancy. The story is excellent and the fights are a big step up from The Witcher 3, but the narrative, the way Rebel Wolves has constructed the tale of Coen of Laslea, is surprisingly rote.
Ultimately, what we ended up with was another big open-world game not so different from Spider-Man, Horizon or Assassin's Creed, where there are roleplaying nods and lots of time devoted to storytelling, but where the bulk of the agency is mechanical—how you build your character, rather than how you define their personality. Which is fine! It's just not what Rebel Wolves sold us on, or what I was hoping for from a story-driven RPG.

Unfortunately, this changes surprisingly little. If you let a vrakhir collaborator go free or murder them, it might change how you feel about the character you're playing, but the world itself couldn't care less. Until the epilogue, most choices you make happen in the background, in a vacuum, and the choices you'd expect to have the greatest impact, like how you choose to defeat Brencis, are largely detached from the kind of Coen you've been playing for 40 hours.

I played Coen as wholesome and naive, but I still found myself able to get every ending. It just came down to which route to Brencis I decided to settle on at the last moment. How I comported myself had no impact. And even though I tried to be consistent when it came to how I roleplayed Coen, the voice direction would often take things in a very different direction, transforming, for instance, what appeared to be a neutral statement into an angry criticism.

This is something that often bugs me in voice-acted RPGs. The acting and direction can dramatically change the tone of a line in a way that feels incongruous to the rest of the conversation, and this happens so much in Dawnwalker. It's something CDPR deftly resolved in The Witcher by making Geralt incredibly stoic. Doug Cockle has plenty of range, but when he's playing Geralt it's extremely subtle, which maintains the consistency of each dialogue sequence.

Final countdown

But Dawnwalker has something most RPGs don't: a ticking clock. And while the most obvious benefit is the sense of urgency it blesses the game with, it also seemed like a promising roleplaying mechanic—helping players to better define their version of Coen by determining what's most important to him.

This is felt most keenly in the prologue, before Coen becomes a dawnwalker. You have one day to do some chores before everyone in the village has to visit the church to get drained by their undead rulers. It's impossible to do everything. Do you focus on helping your fellow villagers? Or do you spend the day hanging out with your family? What's most important to your Coen?

Even during this single day, there's a tangible sense of time moving inexorably forwards. For instance, early in the day you'll meet your siblings, who want to spend time with you and go down to the river. If you decline initially, later you'll find that they've gone to the river by themselves, and you can meet them down there, or just continue to ignore them. There's a schedule.

This promise of time's fickle nature is largely done away with after you complete the prologue. You have 30 days to finish the game—if you want to save your family, anyway—but within those 30 days any time pressure is just an illusion. You'll meet people on the second day who want your help, and they'll still be waiting around for you by the 25th day.

In my entire playthrough, outside of the prologue, I only encountered a single quest where I ran out of time. I could have caught up with an old friend who joined the rebels, but once I'd completed all the quests for the organisation, they mobilised to take on Brencis, at which point I could no longer hang out with my pal. According to our guide lead Sean Martin, who completed every quest Dawnwalker offered, he only found one other example of this happening.

So I never had to make any tough choices. Do I hang out with the mean vampire lady and learn more about the monster I'm becoming? Or do I have a magical adventure with the friendly witch who wants to help me save my family? It doesn't matter because I can always do both.

Evening plans

There's definitely an argument for making Dawnwalker's time limit 20 days instead of 30, but I think that might make the adventure feel too rushed. Instead, sticking with 30 days but putting individual quests on a timer would make a lot more sense. This forces you to make decisions about how Coen should spend his time every day, as well as giving NPCs more agency, while still letting you do a lot.

Being made to choose between staging a jailbreak or assassinating a high-ranking soldier is a much more effective way to establish who Coen is compared to the extremely common choice of: drink a barrel of blood or smash a barrel of blood. It also leaves room for meaningful consequences—like discovering the terrible fate of the prisoners if you opted to do the assassination mission instead, and having other characters actually reference it.

What's frustrating is that you occasionally see glimmers of this, like the time of day you do a quest subtly changing how things play out.

When I tried to meet up with the rebels for the first time, I played through it twice: once during the day, and once at night. At night, I found a rebel being harassed by soldiers, who were immediately hostile to me. After I quickly murdered the soldiers, the rebel took me to meet her friends, but I sensed a trap thanks to my supernatural skills, and avoided getting my leg stuck in a snare.

Attempting this in the afternoon, I was actually able to talk to the soldiers instead of killing them immediately. Rather than fighting, I bribed them to leave the rebel alone. But when I was brought to meet her fellow rebels, I walked right into the snare trap.

This was cool! Though it didn't actually matter at all. In vampire form, even though I avoided the first trap, the rebels ended up jumping me and chaining me to a tree. No matter the time of day, the end result was the same.

I also randomly encountered one of the vamp bosses in a cathedral I'd broken into one evening, at which point I could take her out there and then—dropping from the rafters and plunging my claws into her.

Discovering that some characters had lives outside of the quests attached to them was neat, though taking her out early actually undermined the narrative—it meant I would have missed out on all the context that made her character more than simply a ghoulish monster. So I killed her, felt badass for taking her out early, and then immediately reloaded an old save—letting her live until I'd completed the quests building up to our final confrontation.

But both of these encounters gave me a glimpse of what could have been: a game where time forces your hand, where NPCs have routines and deadlines, where it genuinely matters if you do a quest at noon or in the wee hours of the morning. A glimpse of a better RPG.

Clockwork

Most of the time, however, when you choose to do a quest only really changes the mechanics you can take advantage of. Which also means, given the choice, you should usually try to do things at night, when you're stronger and can teleport. Anything requiring witchcraft, meanwhile, can only be done during the day, so you're not really making a choice there. In this way, time becomes a largely perfunctory feature.

When that illusion is broken, The Blood of Dawnwalker becomes incredibly familiar: a checklist of tasks peppered across a big map, which you can largely do in whatever order you fancy. The story is excellent and the fights are a big step up from The Witcher 3, but the narrative, the way Rebel Wolves has constructed the tale of Coen of Laslea, is surprisingly rote.

Ultimately, what we ended up with was another big open-world game not so different from Spider-Man, Horizon or Assassin's Creed, where there are roleplaying nods and lots of time devoted to storytelling, but where the bulk of the agency is mechanical—how you build your character, rather than how you define their personality. Which is fine! It's just not what Rebel Wolves sold us on, or what I was hoping for from a story-driven RPG.

title: Final Fantasy 14's funky new roguelike mode has me hyped for Evercold's combat revamp, which'll be a winner if it's even half as weird
author: Harvey Randall
text:
Terminally Online
(Image credit: Future) This is Terminally Online : PC Gamer's very own MMO column. Every other week, I'll be sharing my thoughts on the genre, interviewing fellow MMO-heads like me, taking a deep-dive into mechanics we've all taken for granted, and, occasionally, bringing in guest writers to talk about their MMO of choice.
I've had a little time to muck around with Final Fantasy 14 's new Beastmaster limited job—for the uninitiated, a limited job is sort of like a minigame. Not an actual class you can take into current raids or dungeons, but a side-activity that uses the game's combat system to create something new.
The Beastmaster can tame and use creatures in combat. And for the first 30 levels, I was mostly just filling out my little book of monsters in a pleasant haze. I like the job's core combat mechanics, which involve pairing up axe strikes with specific monster abilities to form combos, but grinding in the overworld doesn't do much to show that off.
Where the Beastmaster really shines is in the Crucible of the Unbroken, the limited job's roguelike mode.
I was mostly expecting a straightforward list of bosses to push over via FF14 fun, but played-out combat mechanics, and there is some of that demand. But it's mixed with an overarching minigame of strategy and ability usage that has me watering at the mouth for whatever strange, eldritch things Evercold is cooking up.
For context, Evercold will be introducing "Evolved" jobs —a means to escape the game's rote, two-minute cooldown homogenization that's plagued it for years. During the look we've gotten at these, it seems Square Enix wants to reintroduce job identity to each of the existing jobs by giving them something weird.
For example, the Paladin gets defensive abilities they can essentially "parry" with, unlocking huge punishes if they time them moments before a powerful blow lands. The Dragoon will get an ultimate jump ability and, while it is still being deliberated, the developers have teased the idea of giving the Dragoon a 90% damage resistance buff while they're up in the air. The Dragoon is a DPS job. This'd be unprecedented.
But it's hard to tell, with any development studio, where the hype ends and the overpromising begins. Will Square Enix be brave enough to commit? The Crucible of the Unbroken tells me they very much might.
Granted, this is an isolated bit of content off the beaten path, but it's clear that Square's been using it to experiment with job design that's more reactive to the encounter at hand, rather than just hitting the same buttons every two minutes.
You get given 10 of your collected pets to bring with you into your run—while you can bring three into a battle at a time. Each of these critters have a "Trick" ability, which hits a certain elemental damage type (and enables your Axe combos), a "Tempered Release" ability, which is unique to that creature, and a "Borrow" ability, which is unique to that creature's type.
Square Enix Square Enix Square Enix Square Enix Doing well in crucible battles isn't about memorising your rotation by rote—or even by memorising mechanics, really, although the Crucible is punishing if you mess anything up, as any good roguelike should be. It's about bringing specific beasties to specific encounters and using them in specific phases.
For example, one boss I fought had a mid-fight phase in which four flames steadily advanced to the centre, slapping me with a debuff if I didn't kill them in time. They're weak to water, so I brought out my favourite crab bro, borrowed his "you can spam water attacks now" ability, and melted them down.
This extends to a lot of other mechanics, too. If you want to interrupt a cast, you need a specific critter for that. If you want to endure a massive tankbuster, you'll need to borrow a defensive ability from one of your animal friends.
You aren't just deciding which scissor, paper, or rock to use—the crucible forces you to be deliberate in a few ways. Firstly, these bosses constantly output damage. You can choose to have the boss either attack you or your pet, but health loss is permanent and can only be restored by items or campfires.
You don't want to die, because then you fail the run, but you also might want your pet to live for a future battle—or conversely, you might have a (literal) sacrificial lamb. Furthermore, swapping between pets has a long cooldown, so you're going to have a beastie out for a while. It's a little like the game's already-existing Bard job, wherein you have three songs that last for 45 minutes a pop.
It's extremely compelling, and I've legitimately felt like I'm putting together custom strategies for each fight—all the while juggling my own rotation and dancing between AoE danger zones. And it gives me hope that Evercold's new evolved jobs will be super weird, too.
Maybe not just as weird. Obviously, Beastmaster's occupancy as a limited job gives it a lot more room to experiment—but the Crucible does feel like a testing ground for concepts in future raids and fights. I can easily see a world in which a specific set of jobs are able to simply skip entire mechanics because of their unique abilities.
I don't want a puzzle for every old casual dungeon boss, mind—but I do want those same eureka moments where you realise you've got the perfect answer to a mechanic on your action bar, rather than just memorised as 'this particle effect means we stack up, this one means we spread'. If "evolved" combat design is half as experimental as Beastmaster, then Final Fantasy 14 will have finally shaked off the dust .

title: GTA: London 1961 is full of cockney innuendo and harder than a bobby’s helmet
author: Jeremy Peel
text:
Weird Weekend
Weird Weekend is our regular Saturday column where we celebrate PC gaming oddities: peculiar games, strange bits of trivia, forgotten history. Pop back every weekend to find out what Jeremy, Josh, Ted, and Rick have become obsessed with this time, whether it's the canon height of Thief's Garrett or that time someone in the Vatican pirated Football Manager .
In the wake of GTA 6, series veterans will wax nostalgically about the era of Rockstar expansion packs. No sooner had you finished The Lost and Damned, they'll tell their nurse in between spoonfuls of prunes, The Ballad of Gay Tony landed on your hard drive. There was none of this 'waiting a decade for a new GTA' nonsense.
Fewer will remember the first age of Grand Theft Auto, when even the expansion packs had expansion packs. Really—GTA birthed GTA: London, which in turn begat GTA: London 1961. The latter was released for free online in the summer of 1999, where only a subset of disc-spinning PC gamers were ever likely to find it. Which might have been for the best. Because GTA: London 1961 is perhaps the most punishing visit to the British capital ever conceived. Even including 28 Days Later, and the press reception of Meghan and Harry.
(Image credit: Rockstar) The original Grand Theft Auto already demanded a lot from its players—splicing a nascent open world structure with the limited lives and scorechasing of the arcades. To pass a given level, you'd need to complete several back-to-back chains of missions, thereby building a sufficient multiplier to reach the target score. Getting busted would halve your multiplier instantly. And since cops only needed to bump into you to effect an arrest, like a ghost in Pac-Man, you could easily wind up back at square one, with a dwindling pool of missions to pick from.
GTA: London 1961 is perhaps the most punishing visit to the British capital ever conceived.
To this brutal ruleset, the designers of GTA: London 1961 decided to add mission timers tighter than Adam West's batsuit. How does 20 seconds from East Bermondsey to West Southwark strike you? Or 30 from Westminster Palace to the City of London, where the bankers work? Even in GTA's shrunken top-down metropolis, it's an extraordinary ask—only possible if you pick precisely the right route, floor it, and somehow avoid any serious collisions along the way. "You got to be a little faster," explains your cock-er-ney paymaster, helpfully. "Or Harold'll have your guts for gardening with!"
And should you fail, even once? Those same gangsters will throw you out on your arse, ending the mission with no way of recovery. "This ain't some leisurely afternoon stroll with a stunning bird! This is major international crime, and time and crime waits for Norman, as Harold once said! You blew it, you nob!"
(Image credit: Rockstar) I can't help but wonder how Harold can afford to be so picky with his drivers. If he's got Charlie Croker on the other end of the blower, why is he talking to me in the first place? Good riddance.
Except, without the largesse of old Harold, making money in London is no walk in the park. It might be a drive through Hyde Park, knocking down pedestrians in precise combos to try and max out your score the hard way. Or a slow, repetitive shift at the docks, feeding endless stolen cars to the crane in exchange for £100 notes. I scuppered my chances there by rolling an enormous red bus halfway into the Thames, blocking the crane and making future deliveries impossible.
Thankfully, I'm not the first person to be astonished by the obscenity of those mission timers. And GTA: London 1961 belongs to a time when in-game values could be easily tweaked via notepad files buried on your PC. A kind fellow traveller named Duckilous left instructions on the GTA Forums —an added 30 seconds here, an extra 2375 frames there—and it's no exaggeration to say that those simple inputs are transformative. "I am not a modder for the classic GTA games," my saviour writes. "This is something I just figured out in one day."
(Image credit: Rockstar) Duckilous' GTA London: 1961 remains a frantic, frazzling dash through pixellated renderings of some of the world's most famous landmarks. But that extra inch of breathing room makes all the difference. Another half a minute per mission means you actually have time to read what your objectives are before haring off towards them.
That extra inch of breathing room makes all the difference.
You even get a moment to appreciate the, ah, prose: "What the hell are you doing? You left Mr Caukenbolls all alone. Now some gang has kidnapped him. You'd better find him and get him back here, unharmed! A miss is as good as a moron in this game, mate."
Crucially, the added time means you get to complete more objectives, and therefore access more missions further down the chain. Among GTA: London 1961's scenarios are the theft of a rival gangster's clothes during a pond swim, the filming of a bespoke documentary for Harold to watch at home, and the first-ever implementation of driveby mechanics in the series. There's even a bit of Bond-lite cruising in a Jaguar with a union jack paint job, called the Jug Swinger.
(Image credit: Rockstar) But it's all over pretty fast. This, I now realise, is what the vicious timers were likely covering for: a damning scarcity of scripted missions. I managed to complete four of seven and, having failed the others, was left scraping around to make up the shortfall in my level score.
When run over with a 3x multiplier, policemen yield 3000 points each, and I calculated I'd need to pancake only about a dozen to reach the target. But eventually, even the coppers stopped showing up. London's streets turned eerily quiet, as if every last response unit in Scotland Yard had at last been totalled or exploded. The war was over.
In the end, I was combing the city from Camden to Camberwell, searching for one last way to eke out enough damage to sufficiently impress London's criminal class. And eventually, I found it: a tank parked on a football field. The cars and buildings of Westminster rocked with concussive force as rockets flew. Buckingham Palace's window bill for 1962 would be enormous. But I could finally say I'd completed GTA's toughest challenge to date. Give or take a 30 second timer.

title: Square Enix scrambles to fix Final Fantasy 14 bug where new beastmaster could crash entire servers
author: Justin Wagner
text:
Final Fantasy 14's latest job has just hit the proverbial shelves, and you know what that means: emergency maintenance to fix an extremely bizarre bug. On Sep. 8, the same day that the new beastmaster class dropped, Square Enix had to quickly patch out a bug where "if the player's character leaves the area due to a connection loss at the moment the pet uses a weapon skill that restores its master's HP, the server may crash."
Yes, this bug wasn't crashing the player's own game, but the server. While it's a pretty fringe set of circumstances that have to line up, it's easily replicated with a cheeky pull of one's ethernet cable, so it makes sense that Square Enix scrambled to address this before it became a catastrophe.
If you're unfamiliar with the beastmaster, it's one of the game's "limited jobs" along with the blue mage—basically, they are classes that can't be used to clear the main story quest or endgame dungeons, but they get a bunch of unconventional abilities to futz around with. They are broadly accessible side novelties, and with everyone piling in to check out the new one, it could have been a disaster had this bug been allowed to fester.

On Sep. 8, the same day that the new beastmaster class dropped, Square Enix had to quickly patch out a bug where "if the player's character leaves the area due to a connection loss at the moment the pet uses a weapon skill that restores its master's HP, the server may crash."

Yes, this bug wasn't crashing the player's own game, but the server. While it's a pretty fringe set of circumstances that have to line up, it's easily replicated with a cheeky pull of one's ethernet cable, so it makes sense that Square Enix scrambled to address this before it became a catastrophe.
